reviews.one_line_contribution: Holding the bank, query, k and the actual retrieved items fixed, the paper varies only the moment those items are revealed to the agent — episode start versus a state-detected stall — and claims this alone flips experience memory's paired effect on ALFWorld from harm to gain, and that a swept two-parameter stall trigger (stall length n, injection cap M) matches reimplemented learned when-to-retrieve policies while transferring across backbones and to WebShop without relearning.
reviews.closest_prior_work: The Compliance Trap, arXiv:2607.10608 (verified via s2cli `paper`, and returned again by two of my searches). It is the strongest threat because it already owns most of the frame: it varies the injection schedule (step-1-only, persistent, withheld-until-step-3), it already establishes that harm begins at the first exposed decision and compounds, and the proposal's entire mechanism analysis (Entry-Propagation-Recovery) is that paper's instrument, borrowed wholesale. What survives as new is narrow but real: 2607.10608 uses planted task-wrong memory and a fixed step index, whereas this proposal uses organically retrieved non-adversarial items and an agent-state trigger, and asks about a sign flip rather than a harm magnitude. Second threat, on the other sub-claim: MemCon, arXiv:2607.13591 (verified: "Memory as a Controlled Process" — models memory operations as an MDP and learns an online policy that adaptively decides when, what and how much to retrieve, when to inject a distilled plan, and when to consolidate or forget) and RSCB-MC, arXiv:2604.27283 (verified: risk-sensitive contextual bandit over no-memory / top-resolution / summarize / high-precision / high-recall / abstain / ask-feedback in coding agents). Neither is scooped by the proposal, but neither is beaten by it either: they are the targets, and the proposal only ever compares against its own reimplementations of them. Note also, against the proposal's own related-work framing: ReMe's abstract (arXiv:2512.10696, verified) advertises "context-adaptive reuse," which is weaker support than the proposal's claim that ReMe "retrieves once at task start and names context-aware retrieval as future work" — that characterization needs a full-text check before it is asserted in print.
reviews.strongest_objection: Arm B is not a timing manipulation; it is a timing-and-dose manipulation, and this program's own pilot already showed dose is the causal lever (7 items harmful, 3 items harmless). In every episode where no stall occurs, B injects nothing and is therefore identical to arm H (no memory), not to arm A. Since the pilot's start-of-episode injection is net harmful, B can beat A by exactly the amount of harm it avoids by simply withholding memory from the non-stalled stratum — with zero evidence for the proposed 'the agent arbitrates against wrong items using its own trajectory' mechanism. P1, the pre-registered kill criterion for the central claim, is stated on the overall B-minus-A margin, so the headline result is recoverable from pure non-injection. The stratified analysis is mentioned but is not what P1 gates on, and inside the stalled stratum the sample shrinks (the MDE of 2.5-3 points was computed on the full set, not the stratum), so the one contrast that could distinguish the two explanations is the underpowered one. A second, independent version of the same problem sinks the transfer claim: the two transferred numbers (n, M) are not where the domain knowledge lives — the stall detector is, and it is defined out of ALFWorld's privileged environment signals (inventory/location unchanged, invalid-action message). The proposal concedes WebShop 'needs a proxy' without specifying it. Hand-designing a new detector per environment is relearning by another name, so P4's 'transfers without relearning, whereas the learned policies must be relearned' is not an apples-to-apples comparison. Third, smaller: P3 compares success conditional on compliance across arms, which conditions on a post-treatment collider; the pre-registered <10-point compliance-rate guard limits but does not remove the composition difference between who complies at entry and who complies at a stall.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: (1) Make the primary test exposure-matched. Add a yoked control that receives the same items and the same realized number and cap of injections as the stall arm, but at steps drawn from the stall arm's injection-time distribution rather than at the stall itself (a per-episode time-shuffle), plus an entry-injection arm restricted to exactly the episodes that stall under B. Re-state P1 on B-vs-yoked inside the stalled stratum, and power the study for that stratum (roughly 1/sqrt(stall rate) more pairs), not for the full set. As written, arm E (fixed step 3) does not serve this role because it injects in every episode and is therefore not rate-matched. (2) Specify the WebShop stall detector in the pre-registration, before seeing WebShop results, and report P4 both with the transferred (n, M) and with a detector-redesign cost accounted against the trigger — otherwise report the transfer claim as 'two parameters transfer, the detector does not.' (3) Analyze at the task level with cluster-robust or task-stratified McNemar: ~400 held-out tasks re-run at 3-5 seeds is 400 clusters, not 2,000 independent pairs, and the stated MDE is optimistic by roughly the design effect. (4) Replace the conditional-on-compliance odds ratio with a principal-stratification or always-complier-style analysis, or at minimum report the entry/stall compliance sets' difficulty composition. (5) Read RSCB-MC and MemCon in full rather than from abstracts before freezing F1/F2; a 'static matches learned' result built on abstract-level reimplementations will be read as a claim about the authors' code, not about the published methods, and the paper should pre-commit to reporting the reimplementations' absolute numbers against the originals' published ones.
reviews.missing_baseline: A rate-matched random-timing arm: the same pre-retrieved items, the same per-episode injection count and cap M as the stall trigger, revealed at randomly chosen steps yoked to the stall arm's injection-time distribution (equivalently, an entry-injection arm restricted to the stalled subset). Every arm in the plan differs from B in either how much is injected or how often, so nothing in the design separates 'revealed at a stall' from 'revealed less often.' Arm E is a fixed index in all episodes and arm D is every step; neither is exposure-matched. A reviewer will also ask for a stall-triggered arm that injects the same token volume of task-irrelevant filler (a length-only control), since the program has already shown token volume alone moves this metric.
reviews.preprint_collision: No verified collision. Channels: all queries below ran on channel (a), the s2cli literature command (Semantic Scholar + HuggingFace Papers); channel (b) WebSearch was unavailable in this session and WebFetch is blocked, so no query was answered by the web channel. Queries and returns: (1) 'when to retrieve mid-episode injection timing experience memory LLM agent' --recent [s2 ok, hf ok, 13 hits] → 2604.27283, 2606.04315, 2606.04536, 2605.08374 (MemQ), 2603.04549 (A-MAC), 2606.22844 (RaMem); nothing that fixes the items and varies reveal time. (2) 'stall triggered retrieval agent stuck repeated action memory injection' [12 hits] → 2607.10608 (Compliance Trap), 2607.08716 (Proactive Memory Agent), 2607.12893, 2601.11653, plus a cluster of memory-poisoning papers; no stall- or state-triggered injection study of cross-episode experience memory. (3) 'learned policy when to retrieve memory bandit agent static heuristic baseline' --recent [13 hits] → 2607.13591 (MemCon, both channels), 2606.00547 (MERIT, dual-level memory for text-to-SQL, reports beating no-memory, static-retrieval and dynamic-retrieval baselines — the nearest published static-vs-learned comparison, but a different domain and no timing isolation), 2607.21106, 2606.16285, 2601.08323. (4) 'adaptive retrieval trigger agent trajectory failure detection replanning memory' --recent [17 hits] → 2606.05684 (AdaMEM), 2605.24468 (SAM, state-adaptive within-episode history management), 2604.04949 (Learning to Retrieve from Agent Trajectories), 2607.10608 again. (5) 'tuned static heuristic matches learned retrieval policy transfer across backbones agent memory' --recent [9 hits] → nothing making that claim. ID verification: I verified 2607.13591, 2604.27283, 2607.10608, 2606.05684, 2607.08716, 2512.10696 and 2603.07670 through the command. I could NOT individually verify 2606.29178 (TraceRetain), 2604.11407 (GRIP), 2601.01885, 2602.01672, 2501.09292 or 2501.04899; none of these is load-bearing for the novelty argument, so this does not change the assessment. Judging the proposal's own check: it is above average for this pipeline — it names its channels, its exact query strings, which IDs it verified via s2cli versus took from an abstract, and it discloses a WebFetch attempt whose output it discarded. Two real weaknesses in it. First, it declares 'the mechanism search is effectively empty' and then leans on that emptiness; per the rules an empty search is empty, and my five independent searches reproduce the emptiness, but that only means the strongest threat is a near-miss rather than a hit. Second, its recency control on the web channel was the literal token '2026' in the query rather than a date filter, which is not a recency restriction, and it did not verify MemCon (2607.13591) — the paper its second headline claim is aimed at — through s2cli at all, taking it from a web abstract; I verified it, and the verified abstract says MemCon already learns when, what and how much to retrieve and already reports reduced token use, which blunts both the framing and the cost argument the proposal makes against it. The residual collision risk the proposal itself identifies (2604.27283 on the learned-versus-static sub-claim) is correctly identified, and I would add 2606.00547 to it.
